title.narrative: Integrated Shelter & GBV Support for Flood-Affected Communities in Mayendit, Unity State, South Sudan

description.narrative:
Mayendit is one of the counties in Unity State, with an estimated population of 53,000 people (likely higher, as no recent national census has been conducted). The population has further increased due to an influx of returnees entering the county through monitored entry points. The county is comprised of 13 payams and is located at the junction bordered by Lakes, Jonglei, and Warrap States. The community is predominantly pastoralist and has a long history of intercommunal conflict, including cattle raiding and revenge killings. Recurrent severe flooding has further heightened vulnerabilities, leaving the county underserved with only a few humanitarian actors operating in the area. The county experienced its first flash floods in May 2025, which affected three payams—Dablual, Kah, and Mirnyal—impacting approximately 19,252 people, including 6,171 internally displaced persons (IDPs) and 1,001 returnees. In Dablual alone, 6,498 people were affected, among them 2,448 women, 2,143 men, and 1,907 children. Vulnerable groups, such as older persons and individuals with disabilities, face additional challenges in accessing humanitarian aid. Due to heavy rains, the water levels of rivers feeding into the Nile rose drastically, increasing the river’s volume. By 3 August 2025, data from the Relief and Rehabilitation Commission indicated that 10 payams were submerged, affecting 35,980 people (5,990 households), including 25,994 females and 9,993 males. The affected population is in dire need of humanitarian assistance, as the food security and healthcare sectors have been severely disrupted. This has heightened vulnerability levels, placing the county at IPC Phase 4 (Emergency). Displaced populations rely on host communities and informal settlements for temporary shelter and food; however, these resources are now depleted, as host communities have already been stretched by hosting IDPs and returnees.
According to the Food Security and Livelihoods (FSL) Cluster Early Warning Information Sharing #18 (2025), heavy rainfall is forecast in Jonglei, Upper Nile, and parts of Unity State—classified as high-risk areas for flooding based on historical patterns. It further highlights that 23% of South Sudan’s population is exposed to extremely or very heavy rainfall, increasing the likelihood of displacement and humanitarian needs. As the flooding season peaks in late October, it is anticipated that more people will be displaced, with projections suggesting the number of affected individuals could rise to 40,000.
